facts.value: Treasury Management Interim Report 2025/26 — report to East Dunbartonshire Council, Thursday 18 December 2025 (reference EDC/058/25/RC). 11-page paper on disk (doc 15265), read in full. Lead officer: Chief Finance Officer Jamie Robertson (signed at foot of front sheet). Contact officer: Ross Craven, Accountant. Scottish authority — statutory finance officer is a Section 95 Officer per the Local Government in Scotland Act 2003. Treasury advisor: MUFG Corporate Markets, formerly Link (§3.13, page 3). Interim report is one of three cycle reports; the Outturn Report is stated at §1.1 to follow 'shortly after the financial year end' with no forward date. Purpose per §1.1: prepared under the CIPFA Code of Practice on Treasury Management and the CIPFA Prudential Code for Capital Finance in Local Authorities. Same-day meeting also heard 'Annual Outturn Report on Loans Fund 2024/25' at docs 15261-15264 (report + three appendices) — those are prior-year outturn, NOT bundled into this reading (task scope was doc 15265 only).

source.title: Treasury Management Interim Report 2025/26 — East Dunbartonshire Council, 18 December 2025

facts.note: Meeting has passed (today 2026-08-15). ModernGov URL blocked to us via Cloudflare per the trap logged in EMAIL_TEMPLATE.md §8; PDF read from local disk. No forward treasury meeting date is scheduled in the paper.

Paper prints no internal-borrowing figure itself — this is our arithmetic on their Table 3.

source.title: Treasury Management Interim Report — Table 3, §3.19 page 5 (arithmetic on)

facts.note: This is a year-end PROJECTION, not an as-at position. Scottish councils operate the Loans Fund model, which changes how debt is repaid to internal services (annual loan charges instead of English-style MRP) but does not change the CFR/external/OLTL/internal identity. 2.34% is a distinctively low internal-borrowing share against the councils we have read — comparators from our own notes: Camden 63% (E09000007), Cheshire West and Chester 57% (E06000050), Dumfries and Galloway 17.7% at 2024/25 actual (S12000006). Treat the cross-council comparison as directional — the Loans Fund does mean some Scottish councils show a different mix — but 2.34% is unusual in absolute terms regardless of jurisdiction.

facts.value: Table 6 §3.32 page 8. MUFG interest rate forecast as at November 2025 (advisor since MUFG's acquisition of Link's local-authority treasury advisory business). Bank Rate: Dec-25 4.00% → Mar-26 3.75% → Jun-26 3.75% → Sep-26 3.50% → Dec-26 3.50% → Mar-27 3.50%. 5 Year PWLB: 4.70 / 4.50 / 4.40 / 4.30 / 4.30 / 4.30. 10 Year PWLB: 5.20 / 5.00 / 4.90 / 4.80 / 4.80 / 4.80. 25 Year PWLB: 5.90 / 5.70 / 5.70 / 5.50 / 5.50 / 5.50. 50 Year PWLB: 5.60 / 5.40 / 5.40 / 5.30 / 5.30 / 5.30. Table header does not specify 'certainty' or 'standard' basis. §3.33 page 8: 'Public borrowing remains above forecast due to weaker tax receipts and higher spending, fuelling speculation of further fiscal tightening in the Autumn Budget. Gilt yields have been volatile, rising above 5.5% in August before easing back, reflecting concerns over inflation persistence and the UK's fiscal position.' §3.34 page 8: 'Overall, the outlook for local authorities is one of elevated borrowing costs but stronger investment returns compared to recent years, within a still-uncertain macroeconomic environment.'

source.title: Treasury Management Interim Report — Table 6 §3.32 page 8; §3.33-3.34 page 8

facts.note: Basis (standard vs certainty) is not labelled in the paper — but §3.14 confirms the Council qualifies for and uses the certainty discount, so a certainty comparison is defensible. Sister paper for Dumfries and Galloway (S12000006) explicitly labels MUFG-quoted rates as certainty; this paper does not. Kept ambiguous in the email — both bases quoted.

facts.value: Table 6 forecast for Sep-26 (which is closest to today) against DMO curve at notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026. 5-year: forecast 4.30% vs today's certainty 5.34% / standard 5.54% (+104 to +124bp). 10-year: forecast 4.80% vs today's 5.83% / 6.03% (+103 to +123bp). 25-year: forecast 5.50% vs today's 6.46% / 6.66% (+96 to +116bp). 50-year: forecast 5.30% vs today's 6.27% / 6.47% (+97 to +117bp). Bank Rate: forecast 3.50% vs today 3.75% (+25bp). Every quoted tenor is roughly 1 percentage point higher than the November 2025 forecast for this point in the year. Consistent with the pattern we have seen at every Nov-25 / Dec-25 forecast we have read: the market has moved the same way against Dumfries and Galloway's 22 December 2025 MUFG view (44-53bp) and against multiple English forecasts of the same vintage.

source.title: OUR file — canonical DMO PWLB certainty curve, notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026

facts.note: The move is not distinctive to East Dunbartonshire — every November/December 2025 MUFG forecast we have read has been overtaken the same way. However it is highly relevant to the Council's short-first strategy stated at §3.2: taking short today with a plan to refinance long later when rates 'have fallen' assumes precisely the fall MUFG projected. Nine months on that fall has not happened. Rates are higher, not lower.

facts.value: Independent of the level, today's DMO certainty curve has a steep positive term premium: 1-year approximately 4.95%, 5-year 5.34%, 10-year 5.83%, 25-year 6.46%, 50-year 6.27%. Spread 1y to 25y is roughly 150bp. This means that the shape decision at §3.2 (short-term borrowing prioritised where it offers a cost advantage) is directly supported by today's curve on a level-cost basis — short is cheaper. The refinancing risk (that short-dated borrowing has to be rolled at whatever rates are available when it matures) is the offsetting consideration and is what the November 2025 forecast expected to resolve favourably by 2026-27.

source.title: OUR file — canonical DMO PWLB certainty curve, notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026

facts.note: Two things are true at once: today's shape supports the strategy (short is cheaper); today's level contradicts the forecast that motivated it (long rates haven't fallen). The distinction matters — the strategy makes sense at the point of borrowing; the risk is where the £48m temporary + the maturing debt lands when it has to be replaced.

facts.value: §3.14 page 4: 'Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) long-term interest rates look likely to remain at a stable level for some time, The Council also qualifies for the PWLB Certainty Rate, a discount of 0.20% on all PWLB interest rates, with 0.60% if HRA.' MATCHES our published discount exactly: standard less 0.20% = certainty for general use; less 0.60% for HRA-eligible.
facts.note: One-line cross-check with the paper. Small point but confirms the paper's rate basis and gives a factual line the reader can verify. §3.14 also asserts that PWLB rates 'look likely to remain at a stable level for some time' — nine months on that is the second falsifiable statement in the paper that has not held (25-year certainty has moved from ~6.06% at Nov-25 spot on our estimate to 6.46% today).

facts.value: OUR PWLB file for EAST DUNBARTONSHIRE COUNCIL at 2026-03-31 (from price_book.py): 111 loans outstanding; principal £385,508,974; weighted rate 4.2180%; profile mix MATURITY 63 / EIP 43 / ANNUITY 5. Maturity buckets at 2026-08-15 (108 live loans, £281,758,973): under 12m 27 loans £86.250m at 4.662%; 1-2y 22 loans £98.674m at 4.471%; 2-5y 7 loans £12.250m at 5.667%; 5-10y 8 loans £19.621m at 6.043%; 10-25y 6 loans £18.164m at 4.370%; 25y+ 38 loans £146.800m at 3.375%. RECONCILIATION AGAINST THE PAPER: NOT POSSIBLE against a PWLB-only figure — paper prints no loan-by-loan or PWLB-total anywhere. Paper's Table 3 Borrowing figure of £481.285m (revised year-end projection) is an all-instrument aggregate: PWLB plus market/salix/bank borrowing plus temporary. Residual against our £385.5m PWLB is ~£95.8m, of which the paper accounts for £48m as temporary (§3.32) — leaving ~£47.8m as other long-term borrowing (Salix, bank, other) plus any further borrowing anticipated in H2 (§3.2). Paper does not itemise so the residual is arithmetical, not verified.
facts.note: RECONCILIATION FAILED not because the paper is wrong but because the paper does not print a comparable PWLB-only figure. This is a covering-style disclosure — Table 3 is set for prudential-indicator purposes and reports Borrowing at aggregate. Consequence for the email: no loan-book figure quoted, no loan-count claim, no weighted-rate claim, no residual claim. Follow the template rule: 'when it fails, simply leave the loan-book claim out of the email entirely'. Recorded here in the note where it belongs. Also see loan_book_start_date_caveat below — the bc-loans start dates for this council are all bunched in H2 2025-26 and cannot be used as drawdown dates, which means as-at time-slice reconciliation is not trustworthy for this council either.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep the data and training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on the Interim Report you took to Council on 18 December, ahead of whenever the 2025/26 Outturn Report your paragraph 1.1 refers to lands. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your Interim is short by convention and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

One cross-check first. Your paragraph 3.14 quotes the PWLB Certainty Rate discount as 0.20% on all general PWLB rates and 0.60% for HRA. That matches what we publish exactly — a small check but the sort of thing that would give the game away if we had it wrong.

The reason we wrote is your Table 3. Taking the revised year-end estimates for 2025/26, CFR of £559.984m against Borrowing of £481.285m and Other Long-Term Liabilities of £65.581m leaves £13.118m of internal borrowing — 2.34% of CFR. Between the Original and Revised columns, borrowing rises £12.240m while CFR falls £1.827m, so internal borrowing narrows by roughly £14m in a single revision. Almost every additional pound of General Fund capex this year is planned to be funded externally.

Of the councils we've read, 2.34% is the lowest internal-borrowing share we've come across. For context: Camden runs about 63% of its CFR internally, Cheshire West and Chester about 57%, and Dumfries and Galloway 17.7% at 2024/25 actual. Scottish councils operate the Loans Fund which changes how debt is repaid to internal services rather than through English-style MRP, and that can shift the mix — but 2.34% is unusual in absolute terms whichever accounting model is in use. Not a criticism: an aggressively external position is a real strategic choice and removes the internal-cash constraint that makes the maturity ladder awkward at several of the councils above. It does mean the refinancing point — where the £48m of temporary borrowing at paragraph 3.32 and any short-dated 2025/26 drawdowns need to be replaced — is set by whatever the market is doing at the time, not by cash you can choose to term out.

Which is why your Table 6 caught our eye. Your MUFG forecast from November 2025 has Bank Rate falling from 4.00% at the report date to 3.50% by September 2026 and held there, with long-dated PWLB at 5.50% (25-year) and 5.30% (50-year) by the same point. Paragraph 3.14 goes further and says PWLB long-term rates 'look likely to remain at a stable level for some time'. Paragraph 3.2 explains the short-first borrowing decision by reference to that forecast — short today, on the expectation that longer rates will be lower when the time comes to term out.

Against the DMO's certainty curve this afternoon (notice 314/26 PM, 14 August), Bank Rate is 3.75% and PWLB is 5.34% at 5 years, 5.83% at 10, 6.46% at 25 and 6.27% at 50. Every tenor is roughly a full percentage point above where November had it for this point in the year (a little more on a standard-rate basis before your 0.20% discount). This isn't a critique of MUFG — every November-2025 forecast we've read has moved the same way, so it's a system-wide miss — but it matters here because the short-first strategy sits on it, and nine months on long rates haven't fallen.

Two things are worth separating. Today's curve shape still supports the strategy: 1-year certainty around 4.95% against 25-year 6.46% is a 150-point spread that makes short cheaper on a level basis. The level of today's long end contradicts the forecast that motivated the strategy: the fall the paper is waiting for hasn't happened.

What we publish that speaks to this isn't another forecast — it's the market's own implied path, the SONIA/OIS curve, updated daily, plus the DMO's certainty and repayment curves at both fixings. Not to predict where rates go next; to show where they've moved since your reference date, which no interim paper can do on its own. It's at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. Between now and the 2025/26 Outturn, the daily view lets you write a plain statement of where the November forecast has landed without commissioning anything.
